findings.location: sections/40-household-work.tex:31, on Augustine and Bellarmine at Psalm 79
findings.problem: The contrast gives Augustine the continuity of the original vine and Bellarmine a better Church in its place. Bellarmine himself holds both ideas together. In explanation 14 he says the old vineyard survived its reform, identifies the apostles and Peter’s converts as Israelites, and cites the Gentiles grafted onto Israel’s olive tree. In explanation 15 he calls Christ the chief husbandman and speaks of a better Church. Augustine §9 likewise invokes Abraham’s seed, the graft and Christ. Omitting Bellarmine’s first step makes their answers seem further apart on Israel’s continuity than their texts warrant.
findings.required_result: Give Bellarmine’s reasoning across explanations 14–15. Compare the distinct emphases that survive the shared account of grafting and fulfillment in Christ. Keep both Christian interpretations distinct from the psalmists’ appeal for their own vine.

findings.location: sections/40-household-work.tex:15–19 and 42, on Chrysostom and Thomas in 1 Corinthians 1
findings.problem: At line 17 the claim that Chrysostom proposes two possibilities, followed by the reassurance about inventing a compliment, leaves out his express qualification at the cited locus. In Homily II §4 he also allows collective language about the greater part. In §5 he explains why Paul opens gently, whom the apparent praise actually belongs to, and how it prepares the weaker hearers for correction. At line 19 Thomas’s account of charity becomes a speaker’s decision to make a talent useful. In §86234 on v. 5 he cites Augustine on the person who loves the Church’s unity and relinquishes envy. At v. 7 he separately explains the distribution of gifts among different people. The study’s classroom example shows a benefit of service but misses how even the person without the ability already shares in another’s good.
findings.required_result: Keep the temporal and personal answers as examples from Chrysostom, acknowledge his collective usage, and teach why thanksgiving to God can secure a hearing for correction. Give Thomas’s distinction between distribution and participation through charity, with the reference spanning vv. 5–7. Identify the speaker and learner as an application, and carry the distinction into the moral distillation.

findings.problem: The account of the texts as heard at Mass says the speakers imagine mountains melting. The dated U.S. Isaiah has the mountains quake, while melting belongs to Challoner 64:1, 3. The same treatment leaves open who broke down the vineyard enclosure, although the full psalm directly asks God why he did it (Challoner Ps 79:13). That question matters for an interpretation of apparent divine responsibility. The statement that Paul names only one group of addressees similarly overstates Jerome’s point. First Corinthians 1:2 expressly mentions those who invoke the Lord everywhere as it addresses Corinth.
findings.required_result: Distinguish the two mountain images where the text is first explained. State whom the psalmist questions about the breach, separating this contextual verse from Sunday’s strophes. Present Jerome’s comparison through the mixture of people within the Corinthian church, leaving the wider greeting intact.

findings.problem: Jerome’s physician conceals a frightening instrument before treatment (In Isaiam XVII, p. 151). The study adds a patient reflecting afterward on what the concealment meant and narrates this inside Jerome’s illustration. In the comparison, Augustine’s converted thief learns to provide for the neighbor he formerly robbed. Enarratio 84 §12 contrasts taking another person’s property with giving to somebody who lacks what the former thief now has. It does not identify the recipient as the former victim. The identification shifts the closing comparison toward restitution after the first interpretation explained a further change in desire.
findings.required_result: Keep Jerome’s doctor, patient, concealed instrument and reason for concealment, with any imagined later reflection identified as the study’s or removed. Describe Augustine’s two actions without making the giver’s former victim the recipient. The comparison can then distinguish the changed desire to give from Bellarmine’s identification of the fruit with Christ.

findings.problem: The exposition repeatedly instructs the reader to notice, consider, look at or think of the next point. These stage directions introduce some of the study’s best evidence but make the reader repeatedly wait for the sentence that actually states it. The device recurs through both interpretations and even opens the closing comparison.
findings.required_result: Let the speaker, textual detail or example begin its own sentence. For treatment line 27, use ‘Paul thanks God for the Corinthians’ speech and knowledge.’ For the first interpretation line 21, use ‘The people ask for life before they promise to call on God.’ At the thief, name what Augustine says gave him pleasure. Apply the same edit at the other listed lines while keeping the evidence and credit for each illustration.

findings.location: sections/30-turned-to-god.tex:19–21, the turn from Isaiah to Psalm 80
findings.problem: The study connects Isaiah’s confession with the plea to see God’s face through Augustine. There is also a particularly close precedent in the cited passage of Jerome. At the end of his commentary on the hidden face (In Isaiam XVII, p. 158, immediately before the clay), Jerome himself invokes Psalm 79:4. The reader misses an instance of one biblical prayer already being read beside the other.
findings.required_result: Consider identifying Jerome’s own appeal to Psalm 79:4 beside the study’s application of Augustine. Preserve the distinction between Jerome citing a psalm while explaining Isaiah and the editor interpreting the two appointments together at this Mass.

lanes.title: The people who ask God to turn them
The work the master leaves in the house

summary: I reviewed the complete rights-limited U.S. Advent I, Year B study against the authorized identity, the Missal and Lectionary evidence, Challoner and the cited commentaries. Jerome’s mixed congregation and Augustinian dependence on grace, and Bede’s move from the pastor to each heart at Mark 13:37 (lines 404–405), become intelligible in the prose, but the comparisons, several source details and a recurring editorial device require revision before acceptance of the source edition.
